title: A mixed interview set
objectives: Solve a mixed set of puzzles against a clock, explaining each aloud.

screens.title: Short calculations
screens.prose: Twenty unlabelled puzzles from every level, in three styles: short, multi-stage and strategic. Give each short one about a minute, on your own clock. Say each argument aloud before you type. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the seven answers.

rows: A fair 5-sided die is rolled until every face has shown. Expected rolls?
12 coats are handed back at random. Expected number returned to their owners?
10 fair flips. Expected number of places where HH occurs, overlaps counted?
Expected rolls of a die until two sixes in a row?
A test flags 95% of the 2% who are ill, and 10% of the rest. Chance a flagged person is ill?
Fair £1 bets from £4, stopping at £0 or £12. Chance of reaching £12?
Expected largest of four uniform draws on $[0, 1]$?

hints.text: Name each family before you compute.
Coupons, hats, indicators, a pattern wait, Bayes, ruin, a maximum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Not $5^2$: the waits for each new face are $\tfrac55 + \tfrac54 + \dots + \tfrac51 = \tfrac{137}{12}$.
byKey.r1c1: Each coat comes back with chance $\tfrac{1}{12}$, and there are 12.
byKey.r2c1: There are 9 adjacent pairs in 10 flips, each HH with chance $\tfrac14$.
byKey.r3c1: Not 36: a miss after one six restarts the wait, so $6 + 36 = 42$.
byKey.r4c1: Not 0.95: divide the true flags, 0.019, by all flags, 0.117.
byKey.r5c1: A fair game keeps the mean at £4: $12P = 4$.
byKey.r6c1: The largest of $n$ uniforms has mean $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$.

explain.text: Each answer is one line once the family is named. The coupon wait is $\tfrac{137}{12}$ and the Bayes answer $\tfrac{19}{117}$. The others are linearity, a pattern chain, ruin and the maximum.

screens.title: Which method?
screens.prose: Recognising the family is half the answer. Five ants on a one-metre stick walk at 1 m a minute in random directions. Two ants that meet both turn back.
screens.question: Which idea finds the longest time until all have fallen off?

options.text: Pretend the ants pass through each other
First-step analysis on the ants' positions
options.why: The state space is huge. The swap trick removes it.

options.text: Linearity with one indicator per ant
options.why: Indicators give expected counts, not the longest time.

options.text: Backward induction from the last ant
options.why: There is no choice to make. The motion is fixed once directions are set.

hints.text: What changes if two meeting ants swap labels?
Nothing you can see: the set of positions is the same.
So each ant falls within one minute.

feedback.correct: Pass-through symmetry: at most one minute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ignore the labels on the ants.

explain.text: Swapping labels at each meeting leaves the positions unchanged. So the ants behave like ghosts walking straight on. The last falls off within one minute, whatever the start.

screens.title: Multi-stage: two coins
screens.prose: About 4 minutes. A bag holds a fair coin and a two-headed coin. You pick one at random and flip it twice: two heads.

state.caption: Pick a coin, then flip it twice.

screens.question: What is the chance the next flip of the same coin is a head? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Stage one: update the chance it is the two-headed coin.
Stage two: $\tfrac45 \times 1 + \tfrac15 \times \tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Update the coin first, then predict.

byKey.prior: You skipped the update. Two heads make the two-headed coin likelier.
byKey.post: That is the chance of the two-headed coin. A fair coin can still give a head.
byKey.half: You treated the coin as fair. The two heads are evidence.

explain.text: Two heads have chance $\tfrac12$ with the two-headed coin and $\tfrac18$ with the fair one, so its chance is $\tfrac45$. The next flip is a head with $\tfrac45 + \tfrac15 \times \tfrac12 = 0.9$. A simulation of 200,000 picks gives 0.9001.

screens.title: Which method?
screens.prose: A gambler with £255 bets £1 on a fair coin and doubles after each loss. He stops at the first win.
screens.question: Which idea settles whether this beats the coin?

options.why: Kelly sizes a bet with an edge. Here there is no edge to size.
Symmetry shows each flip is fair, but not what the doubling does.
That only unrolls the cycle. Optional stopping finishes it at once.

hints.text: Is the game fair, and is the bankroll finite?
Yes and yes.
So the expected gain is 0.

feedback.correct: Optional stopping: the expected gain is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a stopping rule can do to a fair game.

explain.text: The bankroll funds eight bets, so the cycle loses £255 with chance $\tfrac{1}{256}$. That cancels the £1 won otherwise. Optional stopping says so without any arithmetic.

screens.title: Strategic: forty matches
screens.prose: About 3 minutes. Two players take 1 to 5 matches in turn from a pile of 40. Whoever takes the last match wins. You move first.
screens.question: How many do you take?

hints.text: Which piles lose for the mover?
With takes of 1 to 5, the multiples of 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Leave a multiple of 6.

byKey.five: Taking 5 leaves 35. Your rival takes 5 and hands you 30.
byKey.one: Taking 1 leaves 39. Your rival takes 3 and hands you 36.

explain.text: With takes of 1 to 5, multiples of 6 lose for the mover. Take 4 to leave 36. Then answer each take of $x$ with $6 - x$.

screens.title: The quick answer
screens.prose: About a minute. Draw uniform numbers on $[0, 2]$ and add them up until the total exceeds 2.
screens.question: What is the expected number of draws?

options.why: That is the quick answer: each draw averages 1. But after two draws the total is often still below 2.
Three is too many. Sometimes two draws suffice, and the mean sits between.
Scaling the draws and the target by 2 changes nothing. The answer is the same as on $[0, 1]$.

hints.text: Divide everything by 2.
Now it is uniforms on $[0, 1]$ exceeding 1.
That expected count is $e$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rescale to uniforms on $[0, 1]$.

byKey.b: You took the quick answer: two draws of mean 1. Two draws stay below 2 half the time, so more are needed.

explain.text: Halve every draw and the target: the puzzle becomes uniforms on $[0, 1]$ exceeding 1. Its answer is $\sum 1/n! = e$. A simulation of 200,000 runs gives 2.7185.

screens.title: Which method?
screens.prose: Two traders arrive at random times within the same hour. Each waits 15 minutes for the other.
screens.question: Which idea solves it fastest?

options.text: Shade an area in the unit square

options.why: Nothing is being updated. The two times form a point in a square.
There is no chain of states here. It is one random point.
That gives expected counts. This asks for one chance.

hints.text: Draw both arrival times as one point.
They meet when the times differ by at most a quarter of the hour.
That is a band about the diagonal: $1 - (\tfrac34)^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture both times as one point.

explain.text: The two times are a uniform point in the unit square. They meet in the band $|x - y| \le \tfrac14$, of area $1 - (\tfrac34)^2 = \tfrac{7}{16}$. The method is the answer's shape.

screens.title: Not enough to go on
screens.prose: About a minute. A bag holds red and blue balls. You draw two at random and both are red.
screens.question: What is the chance the next draw is red?

options.text: Ask how many balls there are and how the bag was filled

options.why: You assumed equal numbers. The puzzle never said so.
That rule assumes every mix was equally likely to begin with. Nobody said so; ask.

options.text: 1, since every draw so far was red
options.why: Two reds do not rule out blue balls.

hints.text: What would you need to compute the chance?
The number of each colour, or how the mix was chosen.
Without it, the honest answer is a question.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can the chance be computed from what you were told?

explain.text: With 3 red and 1 blue the next is red with $\tfrac12$; with 9 red and 1 blue, $\tfrac78$. Without a count or a prior, any number is a guess. Interviewers reward the question.

screens.title: Short calculations, again
screens.prose: Six more short ones, about a minute each, on your own clock. Say the family first. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the six answers.

rows: Five random points on a circle. Chance they all lie in one semicircle?
Two people arrive at random in an hour; each waits 20 minutes. Chance they meet?
A needle of length 1 falls on lines 2 apart. Chance it crosses a line?
Two uniform points on $[0, 3]$. Expected distance between them?
Players alternate rolls of a 4-sided die; the first 1 wins. The first player's chance?
An even-money bet wins with chance 0.65. Kelly fraction?

hints.text: Semicircle, meeting, Buffon, distance, who wins, Kelly.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: The meeting band has area $1 - (\tfrac23)^2$, not $\tfrac13$.
byKey.r4c1: Alternating is not even: the first player wins with $\tfrac{1}{2 - p}$.
byKey.r3c1: On $[0, L]$ the mean distance is $\tfrac{L}{3}$.

explain.text: Each is a one-line formula once the family is named. The semicircle gives $\tfrac{5}{16}$ and the meeting $\tfrac59$. Buffon gives $\tfrac1\pi$, the distance $\tfrac33 = 1$, the dice $\tfrac47$ and Kelly $0.3$.

screens.title: Multi-stage: three rolls
screens.prose: About 4 minutes. Roll an 8-sided die up to three times. After each roll you may stop and take its value in pounds.

state.caption: Each row uses the value of the row above.

screens.question: What is the game worth with best play? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Work back from the last roll, worth 4.5.
With two rolls left, stop on 5 or more: $\tfrac12 \times 6.5 + \tfrac12 \times 4.5 = 5.5$.
With three left, stop on 6 or more: $\tfrac38 \times 7 + \tfrac58 \times 5.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value the last roll first, then step back.

byKey.two: That is the two-roll value. A third roll raises the bar to 6.
byKey.eight: You cannot count on an 8. Stop when a roll beats the value of rolling on.

explain.text: The last roll is worth 4.5 and two rolls 5.5. With three, stop on 6, 7 or 8: $\tfrac38 \times 7 + \tfrac58 \times 5.5 = \tfrac{97}{16}$. A simulation of 200,000 games gives 6.058.

screens.title: Strategic: choose second
screens.prose: About 3 minutes. Penney's game: the interviewer picks HTT, then you pick a pattern of three flips. First to appear wins.
screens.question: Which pattern do you pick?

options.why: THT against HTT is an even race. You can do better.
TTH loses three times in four: HTT needs only the H that must come first.
HHH wins only $\tfrac25$. Three heads in a row is slow.

hints.text: Take the opposite of their middle letter.
Their middle letter is T, so start with H.
Then their first two letters: H, HT, giving HHT.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build your pattern from the front of theirs.

byKey.c: TTH is beaten: any H before TT lets HTT finish first.

explain.text: The opposite of their middle letter, then their first two letters, gives HHT. It beats HTT with chance $\tfrac23$. The node equations or Conway's numbers confirm it.

screens.title: A mock first round
screens.prose: Practise this aloud. Interviewer: "You bought £40 of a team at 4 to 1. The other side now trades at evens. What do you do?" You: "I can lock in a profit by betting on the other side." Interviewer: "How much profit?"
screens.question: What profit can you lock in, in pounds?

hints.text: You win £160 or lose £40 unhedged.
$h = 100$, so the profit is £60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equate the two outcomes after a hedge of $h$.

byKey.hedge: That is the hedge. The locked profit is $160 - 100$.
byKey.win: That is the unhedged win. The hedge costs £100 of it.

explain.text: Hedging £100 gives $160 - 100 = 60$ or $-40 + 100 = 60$. Then say whether you would hedge at all, given your view of the team. Interviewers mark that reasoning as well as the number.

ideas: Name the family first; the method follows from it.
Say the argument aloud as you go: interviewers mark the reasoning, not only the number.
When a puzzle lacks a fact, ask for it rather than assume one.

formula.name: Five lines to know cold
formula.note: Coupons, alternating turns, Kelly, fair ruin, uniforms exceeding one.

summary.trap: Giving the quick answer: $\tfrac12$ for alternating turns, 2 for uniforms exceeding a target, $n^2$ for coupons.

quiz.question: Which idea finds the expected number of different faces seen fastest?

options.text: One indicator per face, and linearity

options.why: That works, but it takes six equations. Indicators take one line.
Symmetry tells you each face is alike, which indicators then use. Alone it gives no number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each face contributes.

explain.text: Face $k$ appears with chance $1 - (\tfrac56)^6$. Adding six of these gives about 3.9906. Linearity needs no independence.

quiz.prose: A bet pays 4 to 1 and wins with chance 0.3.
quiz.question: What is the Kelly fraction? Give four decimal places.

byKey.evens: You used the evens rule. Divide $q$ by the odds.
byKey.ev: That is the edge per £1. Divide it by the odds.

quiz.prose: An interviewer asks: "A family has two children and one is a boy. What is the chance both are boys?"
quiz.question: What is the best first reply?

options.text: Ask how we learned that one is a boy

options.why: That holds if a particular child was seen to be a boy. The wording does not say.
That holds if a parent said 'at least one is a boy'. The wording does not say.

feedback.correct: Ask how the fact was learned.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which answer depends on facts not given?

explain.text: The answer is $\tfrac13$ or $\tfrac12$ depending on how the boy was revealed. Saying so, then answering both cases, is the strongest reply. It shows you see the hidden assumption.
